name: Atom-wave gravitational wave detector
subtitle: an observatory that warns of colliding stars early

effects.effect: atoms cooled almost to absolute zero behave as a single wave

effect: atoms cooled almost to absolute zero behave as a single wave
how: Today's gravitational-wave detectors catch colliding neutron stars only in their last seconds, too late to point telescopes at the blast. Two clouds of ultracold atoms far apart, each acting as a single wave, are kicked by the same laser beams; a passing ripple in space stretches the gap between them, which shows up in the atoms' waves and catches the slower, earlier stage of a merger weeks ahead.
obstacle: It needs a kilometre-tall vacuum shaft or a pair of satellites, and atom sources far brighter than today's.
why: MAGIS and AION are being built; no atom detector has heard a wave.
real: MAGIS/AION-type mid-band atom-interferometer detectors are proposed and under construction; none has detected a gravitational wave.
